lead: A file format is an agreement about how an image is stored: where the header is, how colour is coded, whether pixels or drawing commands are kept, and how the data is compressed. The format decides which software can open the file and how large it is. Web pages, phone galleries, print shops and animation tools all depend on this choice. This chapter maps the common still-image, vector, document and animation formats, and shows how colour mode, transparency, lossless or lossy coding, and resolution guide the choice.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 raster versus vector graphics and colour models, and Chapter 4.2 media types.

blocks.text: Raster images store a grid of pixels. Vector images store drawing commands: move to a point, draw a line, fill a shape. A file format fixes which of these is written, plus a header with width, height, colour mode, resolution and metadata. It also fixes how the data is packed and compressed. The extension is only a label; the bytes inside decide the real format.

Colour mode is the way each pixel's colour is recorded. RGB stores red, green and blue levels. Grayscale stores one brightness value. Indexed colour, which some syllabi call palette colour, stores a small number that points into a table of colours. CMYK stores cyan, magenta, yellow and black for print. An alpha channel stores transparency, so a pixel can blend with the page behind it.

Lossless compression reconstructs exact pixels. Lossy compression discards detail to make a smaller file. The algorithm details belong to Chapter 4.6. At file level, ask what is stored and what is lost.

blocks.where: S is the file size in bytes; W and H are the pixel counts; B is the average bytes per pixel after compression; O is the header and metadata size. This is a planning estimate; content changes the real size.

blocks.text: BMP is a simple bitmap. It often stores pixels with no compression, so it is large but easy to read. It can hold RGB or indexed colour and is used inside Windows and for small test images, rarely on the web.

JPEG is lossy and built for photographs. It stores RGB or grayscale, usually no alpha, and gives small files for smooth tonal scenes. Sharp text and line art suffer visible blocks and ringing, so JPEG is a poor choice for a logo or a screenshot.

GIF stores indexed colour with at most 256 colours. It supports one transparent colour, not partial alpha, and can hold several frames for simple animation. It suits flat diagrams, small icons and short loops.

PNG is lossless and supports RGB, grayscale, indexed colour and full alpha. It is the safe web choice for logos, screenshots and images with transparency. For a photograph, PNG is often larger than JPEG.

TIFF is a flexible container used in scanning, print and archiving. It can store RGB, grayscale or CMYK, many pages and lossless or lossy data. Print workflows value CMYK TIFF because the file states ink colours, not screen colours.
WBMP is a 1-bit format: each pixel is black or white. It was made for small wireless images and is tiny, but it has no colour or grey levels.

Web images are sized in pixels. Print needs enough pixels per inch, ppi, at the final physical size: a 1200×800 image prints 4×2.67 inches at 300 ppi. At 96 ppi the same file would be about 12.5×8.33 inches, but with fewer pixels per inch.

SVG is a vector web format written as text. It stores paths, shapes, colours and text as drawing commands, so it scales without pixelation. A simple logo as SVG is small and clear at any size; a photograph as SVG is a bad fit because it must embed or trace millions of details.

PDF is a page description format. It can hold vector text, raster images and fonts, and it is used for printing and sharing fixed-layout documents. A PDF is not a single image; it is a program-like page description that a reader renders.

PSD is an editing document format. It keeps layers, masks, adjustment settings and the colour mode, so an editor can reopen and change the work. It is not a delivery format for a web page or a print shop, which expect flattened PNG, JPEG, TIFF or PDF.

Animation formats store frames over time. GIF animation uses the same 256-colour limit and binary transparency; it is common for short loops. APNG is an animated PNG. It keeps PNG's lossless coding and full alpha, so it is better for smooth edges and transparency, but support and file size vary.

For the web, the common still formats are JPEG, PNG, GIF and SVG. Choose by content: photograph to JPEG, flat graphic or transparency to PNG, simple vector to SVG, short simple loop to GIF or APNG. Long video belongs to Chapter 4.5.

examples.question: A web page needs a 1200×800 photograph and a 200×200 logo with a transparent background. Choose a format for each and give a reason. The photograph is saved as JPEG at an average of 0.5 byte per pixel. Find its file size in kB, using 1 kB = 1000 bytes.
steps: Photograph: choose JPEG. A photograph is continuous-tone, and lossy JPEG gives a small file. JPEG has no alpha, but the photograph does not need transparency.
Logo: choose PNG or SVG. PNG supports full alpha and lossless flat colour. SVG is better if the logo is a simple vector and must scale to any size.
examples.answer: JPEG for the photograph and PNG or SVG for the logo; the photograph is 480 kB.

w = 1200
h = 800
bpp = 0.5
pixels = w * h
data_bytes = pixels * bpp
kB = data_bytes / 1000
print(pixels)
print(int(data_bytes))
print(kB)

traps: JPEG is for photographs, not line art or text. Its lossy coding creates blocks and ringing around sharp edges.
GIF has at most 256 indexed colours and only one transparent colour, not partial alpha.
PNG is lossless, so for a photograph it is often larger than JPEG; it is not a smaller JPEG.
A .jpg extension does not prove JPEG coding. The file header and bytes decide the real format.
CMYK is for print, RGB is for screens. Sending a CMYK image to a web page can shift the colours.

quiz.q: Which common web format is lossless and supports full alpha transparency?
quiz.a: PNG. It stores RGB, grayscale or indexed colour with an alpha channel.

quiz.q: Why is JPEG a poor choice for a screenshot containing thin text?
quiz.a: JPEG is lossy and designed for smooth photographs. It discards high-frequency detail and creates ringing or blocks around sharp edges, so text becomes fuzzy.

quiz.q: An image is 800×600 pixels and averages 0.25 byte per pixel after compression. Find its size in kB, with 1 kB = 1000 bytes.
A company logo has flat colours, sharp edges and a transparent background. It must appear crisp on a large poster and on a phone. Which format or formats fit, and why?
quiz.a: SVG is best if the logo is vector: it scales without pixelation and is small. PNG is a good raster fallback with lossless colour and full alpha, but its pixel dimensions limit poster sharpness. JPEG and GIF are weaker: JPEG is lossy and has no alpha; GIF has at most 256 colours and only binary transparency.

quiz.q: What does indexed colour, also called palette colour, store in each pixel?
quiz.a: A small index number that points to an entry in a colour table, not the full RGB value.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a PSD file and a PNG file for delivery?
quiz.a: PSD is an editing document that keeps layers, masks and adjustments; PNG is a flattened delivery image with lossless coding and alpha. A web page or print shop normally needs the flattened file.

quiz.q: A file is named photo.jpg but opens as a PNG. What does the extension prove?
quiz.a: Nothing about the codec. The extension is a label; the file header and bytes decide the real format. Software should inspect the header.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer web formats such as WebP and AVIF offer lossy and lossless modes with alpha, and browsers choose them when supported. Image metadata such as EXIF in JPEG and TIFF can carry camera model and GPS location, which raises privacy issues when photos are posted. PDF/A is an archiving profile that restricts features so documents render the same years later. Search for WebP, AVIF, EXIF privacy and PDF/A if you meet these in a project.
